lesson.title: The Hippocampus: The Brain's Memory Librarian
lesson.summary: The hippocampus, a limbic system structure, is essential for converting short term experiences into stable long term memories and for building a cognitive map of familiar spaces.
lesson.body:
The hippocampus is a curved, seahorse shaped structure within the limbic system, with one copy sitting in each hemisphere of the brain. Its central job is not storing memories permanently but building them in the first place: the hippocampus takes fleeting, short term experiences and gradually converts them into stable, long term memories that can eventually be stored elsewhere in the cortex, a process called consolidation.

The clearest evidence for this role comes from one of the most cited case studies in the history of psychology. A patient known widely by his initials, H.M., had large portions of both hippocampi surgically removed in the 1950s to treat severe, otherwise untreatable epilepsy. The surgery controlled his seizures, but it left him almost entirely unable to form new long term declarative memories, meaning he could not reliably remember new facts or events for more than a few minutes, even though his memories from before the surgery remained largely intact and his intelligence and personality were unaffected. His case demonstrated with unusual clarity that the hippocampus is necessary for building new explicit memories but is not where old memories permanently live.

The hippocampus also plays a major, separate role in spatial memory and navigation. It helps construct something like an internal cognitive map of familiar environments, which is part of why damage to this structure can leave people not only unable to form new memories but also disoriented in spaces they should know well.

The hippocampus is unusually sensitive to disruption, which connects it back to several ideas from earlier in this unit. Chronic heavy alcohol use, beyond its direct depressant effects on GABA and glutamate described in an earlier chapter, is strongly linked to a thiamine, or vitamin B1, deficiency that can develop with sustained heavy drinking and poor nutrition. Left uncorrected, that deficiency can damage the hippocampus and nearby structures, producing a severe and often permanent memory disorder with symptoms that closely resemble H.M.'s case: an inability to form new long term memories despite intact earlier ones.

The hippocampus is also notable as one of the few brain regions where evidence points to the ongoing birth of new neurons in adulthood, a process called neurogenesis, rather than a fixed population of cells that only ages and never replenishes. Chronic stress and the sustained cortisol elevation described in the hypothalamus chapter appear to suppress this process and can shrink hippocampal volume over time, one more example of how a hormonal signal that begins in the hypothalamus can reach into a completely different limbic structure and change how it functions.

Together, the hippocampus and hypothalamus illustrate how the limbic system divides its labor. Where the hypothalamus regulates the body's moment to moment physiological needs, the hippocampus manages something more abstract but just as essential to survival: keeping an accurate, continuously updated record of experience that the rest of the brain can draw on later.
